blocks.text: HttpClient returns an Observable, and an observable is lazy — the request doesn't actually go out until something subscribes to it. So subscribe is what fires the call and hands you the result.
Calling http.get(...) on its own does nothing. No subscribe = no request.
But subscribing by hand has two catches:

layers.title: Memory leaks
layers.detail: A subscription keeps listening until it completes or you unsubscribe. A GET completes on its own, but streams (form valueChanges, route params, intervals) don't — forget to unsubscribe and they pile up.

layers.title: Change detection
layers.detail: You manually stuff the result into a field/signal. With OnPush or zoneless, a plain field set can be missed; you end up needing extra wiring to refresh the view.

blocks.text: The async pipe subscribes for you in the template, unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed (no leaks), and tells Angular to update the view when data arrives (no change-detection worries). Keep the Observable in a field and pipe it.

blocks.label: users.ts

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: prefer | async for showing data. If you must subscribe in the class (e.g. to trigger a side effect), add takeUntilDestroyed() so it cleans up.
takeUntilDestroyed() completes the stream when the component is destroyed, so the subscription can't leak. Call it in an injection context (a field initializer or the constructor):

blocks.label: users.ts

blocks.text: Subscribing later (e.g. in ngOnInit or a click handler) is outside the injection context, so pass a DestroyRef: takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef) (with private destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef)).

items: Requests are Observables — they run when you subscribe.
Handle failures with an error handler in subscribe.
Manual subscribe risks leaks (streams) and change-detection misses — prefer | async, which subscribes and cleans up for you.
This works for a small screen; for bigger apps you'd move the calls into a service.
